title: Cities and categories sold
prompt: Marketing wants to know which product categories have sold in which cities. Write `solve(order_items, orders, customers, products)` so it returns each city and category pair once, sorted.
rules: A line counts when its order is in `orders`, that order's customer is in `customers`, and its product is in `products`. The city is the customer's `city`; the category is the product's `category`.
Return each `city` and `category` pair once, however many lines sold it, sorted by `city` and then `category`, both A to Z.
A missing city is still a value and sorts first. Return only `city` and `category`, in that order.
hints: Chain three joins from `order_items`: to `orders` on `order_id`, to `customers` on `customer_id`, to `products` on `product_id`. Inner joins drop lines with any unknown link.
Both `customers` and `products` have a `name` column, but you only need `city` and `category`, so select them right away.
`distinct()` removes repeated pairs; `orderBy("city", "category")` sorts them. Sort last, after `distinct()`.
explanation: Chain inner joins so a line only counts when every link exists: `order_items.join(orders, on="order_id", how="inner").join(customers, on="customer_id", how="inner").join(products, on="product_id", how="inner")`. Then `select("city", "category")`, `distinct()` to keep each pair once, and `orderBy("city", "category")` last, because `distinct` doesn't keep any order. Ascending order puts a missing city first, as the rules ask. Left joins would bring in lines with unknown links as pairs with a missing city or category, and sorting by category first gives the same pairs in a different order.
